name: Chocha-ngachakha
catalog_citation: Tournadre, Nicolas & Karma Rigzin. 2015. Outlines of Chocha-ngachakha: An undocumented language of Bhutan related to Dzongkha. Himalayan Linguistics 14(2): 49-87. DOI 10.5070/H914225395.

catalog_quote: CN is a tonal language with two distinctive tones: high and low registers. In our transcription, only the low tone is marked by a line under the vowel; the high tone is not marked. Like other Tibetic languages, CN is a word tone language, not a syllable tone language like many Southeast Asian languages, such as Burmese, Chinese, Thaï, Vietnamese, etc. The tone reflexes are in general similar to other modern Tibetic languages such as Standard Tibetan or Dzongkha, but there are a few discrepancies, notably concerning the nasals. The tones are usually predictable from the reflexes with CT. For the plosives and affricates, voiced initials are normally realized with a low tone; the unvoiced are pronounced with a high tone ... The aspirated unvoiced are pronounced with a notably lower pitch than the non-aspirated ones; however, they are still perceived as high register. ... As we have seen in…

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both the deciding quotation (sect. 3.3.3, pp. 58-59) and the negation 'stressed' remark (sect. 4.1.3, p. 62) are verbatim in the held at the stated locators. Deciding source: Tournadre & Rigzin 2015 is a grammar sketch but it is the only description of the language in Glottolog (n=1) and, per Wang 2023's own literature statement, the only one in existence; so 'best available held' is yes. Web search (ISCA archive, eScholarship, academia.edu, general) surfaced one additional relevant work, Wang 2023 (TAI 2023, single-speaker acoustic study), downloaded to It confirms a two-register word-tone system and refines it: the initial syllable bears the tone and non-initial syllables are pitch-neutralized; the tone domain is the word. It says nothing about stress. This is consistent with our 'tonal' (word-tone, tonal-OR-PITCH

sources.quote: Abstract (p. 93): 'tone in this word-tone language falls on the initial syllable of a word, and the high or low category of the tone leads the prosodic pattern of the entire word or phrase'. Sect. 3.2.1 (p. 95): 'a distinctively higher pitch falls on the initial syllables of the high-toned words ... However, the pitch is neutralized on the second syllables of all high- and low-toned words.' Conclusions (p. 97): 'The language has a word-tone system, with a contrast of high and low registers. The initial syllable is the bearing unit of the word tone, but the tone type applies to the whole word.
sources.locator: Abstract p. 93; sect. 3.2.1 p. 95; sect. 4-5 pp. 96-97
sources.note: Only acoustic study of the language; establishes that the H/L word tone is borne by the word-initial syllable with non-initial syllables neutralized, which fills our 'domain: not stated by the source' field and supports the tonal (word-tone) coding; our record rests solely on the 2015 sketch's one impressionistic page.
